_note: Where two different hominins were in the same place at the same time, and what came of it. `kind` is one of: admixture (genes moved), hybrid (a first-generation individual), replacement (one disappears where the other arrives), coexistence (long overlap with neither replacing the other), overlap (same region and time, no contact evidenced), conflict (violence, between groups of the SAME species). `c` is confidence in the event itself.

contacts.label: The main Neanderthal admixture
contacts.evidence: Neanderthal genome sequences from Vindija and the Altai compared against living genomes; the length and distribution of surviving Neanderthal segments date the mixing to roughly 50,000–60,000 years ago.
contacts.result: Every living person whose ancestry lies outside sub-Saharan Africa carries about 1.5–2 percent Neanderthal DNA. It is not a trace — it is in the genome of most of the people alive today.

contacts.label: The Denisovan admixture
contacts.evidence: A Denisovan genome from a finger bone, compared against living Papuan and Aboriginal Australian genomes, which carry segments found in no other living population.
contacts.result: Up to about 5 percent Denisovan ancestry in Papuans and other Oceanian populations — the largest contribution from any archaic hominin known, and the reason a finger bone from Siberia changed the prehistory of New Guinea.

contacts.label: "Denny" — a first-generation hybrid
contacts.evidence: A single bone fragment from Denisova Cave, Denisova 11, whose genome carries one Neanderthal chromosome set and one Denisovan set: its mother was a Neanderthal and its father a Denisovan.
contacts.result: Direct proof that the two populations met and had children — from one broken bone. It is also the only first-generation hybrid between any two hominins that has ever been identified.

contacts.label: The West African ghost population
contacts.evidence: Statistical models fitted to whole genomes from Yoruba, Mende and other West African populations, which carry ancestry that matches neither modern humans nor any known archaic genome.
contacts.result: A few percent of the ancestry of some West African populations comes from a hominin that has never been found. There is no fossil, no site and no name — only the signal.

contacts.label: A Neanderthal great-great-grandparent
contacts.evidence: Oase 1, from Peştera cu Oase in Romania, has Neanderthal segments so long that the ancestor they came from was only four to six generations back.
contacts.result: One individual, one family tree, and the clearest single piece of evidence that the mixing was not a single ancient event in the Levant but happened repeatedly, including in Europe, within living memory of the people involved.

contacts.label: Recent Neanderthal ancestry in the earliest Europeans
contacts.evidence: Genomes from Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, among the earliest Homo sapiens in Europe, all carry recent Neanderthal ancestry — and none of those lineages survives in living Europeans.
contacts.result: The first modern humans in Europe mixed with Neanderthals and then died out or were replaced. The people who are the ancestors of later Europeans are a different, later arrival.

contacts.label: Two hominins in one Levantine landscape
contacts.evidence: Nesher Ramla stone tools match those made by local Homo sapiens of the same period, and the authors argue the Ramla population is ancestral to Neanderthals and met modern humans here.
contacts.result: If the reading holds, the Levant was a meeting place 130,000 years ago as well as 60,000 years ago — which means the interbreeding did not have a single location or a single date.

contacts.label: The Neanderthal disappearance
contacts.evidence: Refined radiocarbon dates from forty Neanderthal sites across Europe and the Caucasus, showing the last appearances cluster between about 41,000 and 39,000 years ago.
contacts.result: A species that had held Europe and western Asia for 350,000 years was gone within a few thousand years of modern humans arriving. The cause is not settled, and the pattern is small populations, a changing climate, and a competitor — not one single event.

contacts.label: Mixing dated by segment length
contacts.evidence: The Ust'-Ishim femur from western Siberia has long Neanderthal segments that place the mixing event a few thousand years before he lived, and he has no Denisovan ancestry at all.
contacts.result: Long segments mean recent mixing, and the technique turns a single bone into a date for an event nobody witnessed. Modern humans reached Siberia and mixed with Neanderthals there.

contacts.label: A million years side by side
contacts.evidence: Paranthropus boisei and early Homo fossils in the same sedimentary basins at Olduvai, Koobi Fora and Konso, over more than a million years.
contacts.result: Two hominins shared one landscape for a million years and neither replaced the other. This is the case that makes the whole map worthwhile: coexistence, not a ladder, was the normal state of affairs.

contacts.label: Java — erectus gone before sapiens is known there
contacts.evidence: Homo erectus at Ngandong is dated to 117,000–108,000 years ago. Modern humans are in Sumatra by about 73,000 and in Australia by 65,000, but are not known on Java until much later.
contacts.result: The two were in the same region within about 40,000 years of each other, and no site shows them together. Any contact is unproven — this is marked as an overlap of ranges, not of people.

contacts.label: Flores — probably no meeting at all
contacts.evidence: The 2016 re-dating puts the last Homo floresiensis at about 60,000 years ago and the earliest modern human evidence on Flores at about 46,000 years ago.
contacts.result: On the current dates there is a gap of more than 10,000 years, so the hobbit probably did not meet modern humans at all. That is the honest answer, and it is more interesting than the story it replaces.

contacts.label: Nataruk — a massacre 10,000 years ago
contacts.evidence: Twelve skeletons at Nataruk, West Turkana, Kenya, with stone projectile points embedded in the bone and no evidence of deliberate burial.
contacts.result: The earliest clear evidence of a group killed together by other people. Both sides were Homo sapiens — so it belongs on this map as a warning about what the word 'clash' should mean here.

contacts.label: Jebel Sahaba — a cemetery of the wounded
contacts.evidence: At least 61 individuals from a Late Pleistocene Nile Valley cemetery, with healed and unhealed injuries from projectile points, and re-analysis showing wounds from more than one episode.
contacts.result: Not one massacre but repeated violence across years — probably over land or water as the Nile valley dried. It is a Homo sapiens site, and a reminder that the species that absorbed the Neanderthals also fought itself.
